title: Building Cathedrals
objective: After this level you can explain how medieval builders raised huge cathedrals.
summary: Rib vaults, pointed arches and flying buttresses let Gothic cathedrals rise and fill with windows; master masons and treadwheel cranes built them, partly paid for by tithes.

cards.headline: Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248. It was finished in 1880.
cards.body: That’s 632 years from first stone to last, with a pause of centuries in the middle. How do you build something that takes longer than a lifetime?

cards.headline: Stone that pushes sideways
cards.body: A stone ceiling is heavy, and a vault pushes outward on the walls beneath it. Gothic builders answered with three tools. The pointed arch and the rib vault, where stone ribs carry the ceiling, let them cover taller, broader spaces. The flying buttress, a half arch, carried the vault’s thrust across an aisle to an outer pier. With the push handled outside, walls could open into huge windows. Tradition names Saint-Denis, rebuilt about 1135 to 1144 under Abbot Suger, as the first Gothic building.

mascot.line: Keep this: the push is carried outside, so the walls are free to become windows.

cards.headline: The master mason’s building site
cards.body: A master mason ran the site. He made templates for every shaped stone and put a master craftsman in charge of each part of the job. Canterbury’s builders brought stone by boat from France, easier than hauling it over bad roads. On scaffolding, cranes and pulleys lifted it, some powered by a treadwheel: a “hamster wheel” big enough for two men. And the bills? Tithes were a prime source of money for many great cathedrals.

cards.headline: When the ceiling fell
cards.body: At Beauvais, builders raised the tallest Gothic stone vault in the world. In November 1284 its flying buttresses twisted and broke, and the choir vault came down, probably set off by a storm. Rebuilding took until about 1340. Gothic builders were pushing stone to its limits, and sometimes the stone pushed back.

cards.headline: Building cathedrals: understood
learned: Rib vaults and pointed arches let builders go higher
Flying buttresses carried the thrust and freed walls for windows
Master masons, shipped stone and treadwheels built them

questions.prompt: In a Gothic church, _____ carried a vault’s outward push across an aisle to an outer pier.

options.label: the rib vault
options.rationale: Its ribs carry the ceiling itself.

options.label: the rose window
options.rationale: Windows were what buttresses made room for.

questions.explanation: A flying buttress is a half arch carrying the vault’s thrust across an aisle to an outer pier.

questions.prompt: Match each cathedral-building term with its description.
questions.explanation: In a rib vault, stone ribs carry the ceiling. A flying buttress is a half arch. A treadwheel was a “hamster wheel” big enough for two men, and the master mason ran the site.

questions.prompt: How did the tithe, the tenth paid to the Church, connect to the great medieval cathedrals?

options.label: It was paid in cut stone for the builders
options.rationale: It was paid in money or produce.

options.label: It was a prime source of money for building them
It paid only for the stained glass
options.rationale: It paid for much more than glass.

options.label: Cathedrals were built to store it
options.rationale: Tithes paid for cathedrals, not the reverse.

questions.explanation: Tithes paid the clergy and the poor, and they were also a prime source of money for building many cathedrals.
